props.title: The Gospel According to St. Matthew

sections.content: Pier Paolo Pasolini's The Gospel According to St. Matthew revolutionized religious filmmaking by stripping away Hollywood pageantry for stark neorealist power. Unlike the epic grandeur of The Ten Commandments (1956) or King of Kings (1961), Pasolini shot in the harsh landscapes of southern Italy with non-professional actors, creating an urgent, documentary-like Jesus story. The director's Marxist atheism paradoxically produced one of cinema's most spiritually authentic Christ films, endorsed by the Vatican despite (or because of) its radical approach.

sections.content: The film's influence rippled through subsequent religious cinema. The Passion of the Christ (2004) borrowed Pasolini's use of authentic historical language, while Jesus of Montreal (1989) echoed his parallel between Christ's story and contemporary social justice. Pasolini's documentary-style approach inspired later filmmakers like Of Gods and Men (2010) and Calvary (2014) to explore faith through unvarnished realism rather than spectacle.

Pasolini's casting choices proved revolutionary. Using his own mother as Mary and Spanish student Enrique Irazoqui as Jesus created an immediacy that Hollywood stars couldn't match. The non-professional cast and handheld camerawork make Christ's message feel urgent and present, not distant history. This influenced later films like Son of Man (2006), which reimagined Jesus in contemporary South Africa. SUBHEAD: The Political Christ

sections.content: Pasolini's Marxist reading of Matthew's Gospel emphasizes Jesus as a revolutionary figure challenging authority. This political interpretation influenced liberation theology and films like Mission (1986) and Romero (1989). The director's focus on Christ's confrontations with power structures and defense of the poor resonates in modern religious films like Two Popes (2019), which explores liberation theology's legacy.
